title: 'Shocking': Hospital inquiry urges axing of public-private partnership

Topic:Public Health

A NSW upper house committee has handed down its findings relating to a string of maintenance concerns at a Newcastle hospital.  (Supplied)

A NSW parliamentary inquiry investigating a string of alleged maintenance failures at Newcastle's Calvary Mater Hospital has recommended terminating the public-private partnership.

The inquiry's report was tabled in parliament today along with seven recommendations.

The government has until November 5 to respond to the report's recommendations.

"Shocking revelations" have led to a NSW parliamentary inquiry calling for a Newcastle hospital to be put back in public hands.

The Calvary Mater Hospital, which operates under a public-private partnership, is one of the leading cancer hospitals in regional NSW, with some patients travelling hours to receive care.

But it has been under intense scrutiny over the past 12 months, after a mould infestation was found in the hospital's cancer unit, and maggots were found spread across the hospital floor.

The parliamentary inquiry was chaired by Greens MP Dr Amanda Cohn, who said in a statement the revelations shared by staff and whistleblowers were "shocking".

"We heard about maggots falling from the ceiling onto a patient, nurses funnelling rainwater into garbage bins during the night, a doctor fainting during surgery because of high humidity in the operating theatre, and explosive allegations of falsified maintenance records," she said.

"All these problems could have been prevented.

The report recommends the NSW Government terminate the current public-private partnership and bring ownership and management of the hospital directly into NSW Health as soon as reasonably possible.

It also recommends the Orange and Bathurst Hospital public-private partnerships be analysed for value, including whether services should be returned to direct public management by the Western NSW Local Health District.

The committee heard explosive allegations from staff across three public hearings. (ABC Newcastle: Nakita Jager)

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park has stopped short of putting the hospital back in public hands.

"We are looking at that contract very, very carefully. We are not there yet, and I don't want to give anybody a false hope or false direction that we are."

Mr Park said the government was "willing and able to step in if that is necessary".

"But I've also got a responsibility to make sure that taxpayers' money is spent wisely. And at the moment we have a contract; we are holding those contractors to account."

He said a meeting was held yesterday with Treasury and NSW Health to work through some of the challenges of the public-private partnership contract.

Following the mould discovery, the state government commenced rectification works on the building, including the replacement of non-compliant cladding.

The minister has assured the community the hospital is safe.

"In relation to the issues around fire safety, they were an issue for the private contractor, but we intervened and double checked that, that is safe," he said.

"Every time that there is mould or mould to be removed, we are in there and doing that."

The government has until November 5 to respond to the report.

Health Minister Ryan Park has reassured the community Calvary Mater Hospital is safe. (ABC News: Andrew Whitington )

Honeywell is contracted to look after maintenance at the hospital.

In a statement, the company said it's reviewing the contents of the inquiry report.

"We remain committed to supporting the hospital, its patients and staff, and the broader community, and will engage constructively with all responsible parties to address the matters raised in the report," it said.

In a statement, Health Services Union Secretary Gerard Hayes said the recommendations made by the committee must be implemented urgently.

"Our members at the Calvary Mater have been raising the alarm about mould, potable water failures, intimidation of whistleblowers and a 'sweep it under the rug' culture for close to a decade," he said.

"The committee has listened, and the recommendation that the hospital return to public hands is a moment of accountability.

Mr Hayes said the findings showed a "clear message about the failure of the public-private partnership model in our health system".

"Whether it's the Northern Beaches or Newcastle, staff and patients are put at risk," he said.

"It's time to end the failed experiment."

The ABC has approached Calvary Care for comment.
